title: Vocabulary: precise language for Writing Task 2 arguments
status: Owner approved v1.1.0 on 2026-10-26; teacher release to all eligible schools (optional vocabulary lesson)
rights: Original Brains Heist LLC instructional material, AI-assisted. Passages, people and data are fictional and created for practice. Not official IELTS material. Human editorial and classroom review recommended.
prerequisites: Learners can identify the question type in a Task 2 prompt.
Pitched at learners aiming for Band 6.5-7.5 whose essays rely on 'good/bad', 'very' and 'I think', or overstate claims.

objectives.text: Express a clear position and qualify claims precisely (arguably, to some extent, it is likely that).
Use cause, effect, solution and concession language with the correct preposition and grammar (stem from, have an effect on, although/despite).
Recognise how a writer signals claims, concessions and conclusions in an argument text.

levels.foundation: Use the cause/effect and concession frames in the support box while writing.
levels.core: Write the paragraph with no use of 'good', 'bad', 'thing' or 'a lot of', and with one hedged claim.
levels.extension: Concede one counter-argument with 'Admittedly, ... however, ...' and rebut it.
levels.high_band: Write a full body paragraph in which every sentence advances the argument, with precise vocabulary used only where it fits.

word_bank.example: Long working hours can lead to stress.
Many health problems stem from poor diet.

word_bank.item: tackle / address (a problem or an issue)
word_bank.meaning: take action to deal with a problem

word_bank.example: Noise has a detrimental effect on concentration.

word_bank.item: have a beneficial effect on / be beneficial to
word_bank.example: Exercise is beneficial to mental health.

word_bank.meaning: used to present a careful claim that you can defend
word_bank.example: Arguably, the internet is the most important invention of the century.

word_bank.item: to some extent / to a large extent
word_bank.example: I agree with this view to a large extent.
It is unlikely that cars will disappear soon.

word_bank.meaning: many / a large part of (more precise than 'a lot of')
word_bank.example: A significant proportion of graduates work abroad.

word_bank.item: a key factor in / a major concern
word_bank.example: Cost is a key factor in this decision.
One drawback of online learning is isolation.

word_bank.item: admittedly ... however / although + clause / despite + noun
word_bank.meaning: accept a point, then argue against it
word_bank.example: Although fees are high, a degree usually pays for itself.

word_bank.item: implement / introduce (a policy or a measure)

stages.title: Opening challenge: vague, precise or over-formal?
stages.student: Decide which sentence an examiner would reward most.
stages.teacher: Learners vote; reveal the comments. Focus on precision and control, not long words.
stages.say: Precise words make an argument clearer, not just longer.
stages.check: Learners name two vague words in Learner A's sentence and one problem in Learner C's.

stages.title: Word bank: cause, effect, solution and stance
stages.student: Group the word bank: cause and effect, solutions, stance and concession. Note the preposition or structure after each item.
stages.teacher: Drill: lead TO, stem FROM, an effect ON, although + clause, despite + noun.
stages.say: The preposition and the structure are part of the word.
stages.check: Learners complete five frames with the right preposition.

stages.title: Which word fits exactly?
stages.student: Choose the one correct option. All the options are real English words.
stages.teacher: Six minutes, word bank closed for core and above. In the reveal, ask why each wrong option fails.
stages.say: Check the word, the word after it, and the grammar of the sentence.
stages.check: Learners give the reason for at least four distractors.

stages.title: Reading: who should pay for university?
stages.student: Answer the nine questions in twelve minutes. Mark the phrases the writer uses to give an opinion, concede a point and conclude.
stages.teacher: Twelve minutes, then reveal. Ask learners to read out the stance phrases they marked (In my view, I would argue, It is true that ... but).
stages.say: YES/NO/NOT GIVEN tests the writer's opinion, not the facts.
stages.check: Learners quote the stance phrase that decided each YES or NO answer.

stages.title: Plan a body paragraph
stages.student: Plan: topic sentence, reason, effect, specific example, concession, link back.
stages.teacher: Check that each plan has a specific example.
stages.check: Every learner has a plan with an example.

stages.title: Write independently
stages.student: Write one body paragraph of about 140 words.
stages.say: Use precise words where they help your argument; do not force them.

stages.title: Compare with the model
stages.student: Find the cause/effect, hedging and concession language in the model; improve two phrases in your own paragraph.
stages.teacher: Ask learners to read one improved sentence aloud.
stages.say: The model is illustrative, not a target band.

stages.title: Exit ticket and homework
stages.student: Complete the exit ticket and note the homework.
stages.say: Keep a list of the vague words you over-use and their precise replacements.
stages.check: Every learner writes one hedged claim.

blocks.title: Vague, precise or over-formal?
blocks.mode: Opening challenge; learners decide before the reveal
blocks.instructions: Question: 'Many people work long hours. What problems does this cause?' Three learners wrote the first sentence of a body paragraph. Which is best?

examples.label: Learner A
examples.text: Working a lot is a bad thing because it causes a lot of problems for people.
examples.comment: Vague: 'a lot', 'bad thing' and 'problems' say nothing specific.

examples.label: Learner B
examples.text: Excessive working hours can lead to chronic stress, which in turn may have a detrimental effect on family relationships.
examples.comment: Best: precise words, a clear chain of cause and effect, and careful 'can' and 'may'.

examples.label: Learner C
examples.text: Prolonged occupational engagement engenders multifarious deleterious ramifications for individuals.
examples.comment: Over-formal and unclear: the words are real, but the sentence says less than Learner B's. Examiners reward accurate, natural vocabulary, not rare words used to impress.

blocks.title: Which word fits exactly?
blocks.mode: Controlled practice; word bank closed for core and above
blocks.instructions: Choose the correct option, A, B, C or D, to complete each sentence. All the options are real English words; only one is natural and grammatically correct in this sentence.

items.prompt: Excessive working hours can ______ to stress-related illness.
items.evidence: lead to
items.reason: 'Result' needs 'in'; 'cause' and 'bring' do not take 'to' in this sense.

items.prompt: Many traffic problems stem ______ a lack of investment in public transport.
items.evidence: stem from
items.reason: 'Stem' takes only 'from' in this meaning.

items.prompt: Regular exercise has a beneficial effect ______ mental health.
items.evidence: an effect on
items.reason: The noun 'effect' takes 'on'.

items.prompt: Governments need to ______ the problem of youth unemployment urgently.
items.evidence: tackle a problem
items.reason: You 'undertake' a task, 'execute' a plan and 'conduct' research, but you tackle a problem.

items.prompt: The writer wants to give a cautious opinion of their own: '______, the internet is the most significant invention of the last fifty years.'
items.evidence: arguably = a careful claim the writer can defend
items.reason: 'Supposedly', 'allegedly' and 'reportedly' present the claim as someone else's and suggest the writer doubts it.

items.prompt: In my view, the advantages of studying abroad ______ the disadvantages.
items.evidence: outweigh = are more important than
items.reason: 'Overrule' is used for decisions, 'overtake' for movement or growth, and 'overload' means give too much to.

items.prompt: A significant ______ of graduates now choose to work abroad.
items.evidence: a significant proportion of + plural countable noun
items.reason: 'Amount' and 'deal' are used with uncountable nouns, and 'quantity' is not used for people.

items.prompt: ______ tuition fees are high, a degree usually increases a graduate's lifetime earnings.
items.evidence: although + clause
items.reason: 'Despite' needs a noun or -ing form; 'however' and 'nevertheless' cannot join two clauses in this position.

blocks.title: Reading: who should pay for university?
blocks.mode: Timed practice under test-like conditions: twelve minutes, no dictionary
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-6: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer? Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN. Questions 7-9: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

stimulus.title: Who should pay for university?
paragraphs: In many countries, the question of whether university education should be free at the point of use has become one of the most divisive issues in education policy. Supporters of free tuition argue that higher education benefits society as a whole, and that charging fees discourages talented students from poorer families from applying. Opponents respond that graduates themselves are the main beneficiaries, since a degree tends to increase lifetime earnings, and that it is therefore unfair to ask taxpayers who did not attend university to cover the cost. In my view, both positions contain an element of truth, but neither is as straightforward as its advocates suggest.

Consider first the claim that fees deter disadvantaged students. It seems intuitively plausible, and in some countries the introduction of fees was followed by a fall in applications. Yet the evidence is more mixed than is often assumed. In several systems where fees are high but are repaid only once a graduate's income exceeds a certain threshold, participation among poorer students has continued to rise. What appears to matter most is not the price itself but whether students believe they will be able to manage the debt. Clear information about repayment, I would argue, may do as much to widen access as abolishing fees altogether.

The argument that graduates should pay because they benefit personally is also less convincing than it first appears. It is true that, on average, graduates earn more than non-graduates, but averages conceal enormous variation between subjects and institutions. Moreover, many of the professions on which society depends most, such as nursing and teaching, require degrees but offer relatively modest salaries. Requiring these graduates to repay large debts may discourage people from entering exactly the careers that a country most needs to fill.

There is also a practical consideration. Free tuition must be funded from general taxation, and when public budgets are under pressure, governments that have abolished fees frequently respond by limiting the number of university places. The result can be that access becomes more restricted, not less, since the available places tend to go to applicants from schools that prepare students most effectively for competitive entry.

A more defensible position, in my opinion, lies between the two extremes. Fees could be retained for most courses but reduced or waived for subjects linked to shortages of skilled workers, and repayments could be linked to income so that no graduate is required to pay more than they can reasonably afford. Such a system would not satisfy those who regard free education as a matter of principle. It would, however, address the two concerns that matter most: ensuring that cost does not prevent capable students from applying, and ensuring that public money is directed where it brings the greatest benefit.

items.prompt: Neither side of the debate fully reflects how complicated the issue is.
items.evidence: neither is as straightforward as its advocates suggest
items.reason: The writer says both positions are less simple than their supporters claim.

items.prompt: Charging fees always reduces the number of applications from poorer students.
items.evidence: participation among poorer students has continued to rise
items.reason: The writer gives counter-evidence and calls the evidence 'more mixed than is often assumed'.

items.prompt: Students' confidence about repaying their loans may matter more than the cost of the course.
items.evidence: What appears to matter most is not the price itself but whether students believe they will be able to manage the debt
items.reason: 'Confidence about repaying' paraphrases 'believe they will be able to manage the debt'.

items.prompt: Most taxpayers support the abolition of university fees.
items.evidence: Taxpayers are mentioned, but not their opinions about fees.
items.reason: The writer never says what most taxpayers think.

items.prompt: Making university free can, in practice, reduce the number of people who are able to study.
items.evidence: governments that have abolished fees frequently respond by limiting the number of university places
items.reason: Limiting places means fewer people can study, so access can become 'more restricted, not less'.

items.prompt: Fees should be removed for every subject.
items.evidence: Fees could be retained for most courses but reduced or waived for subjects linked to shortages of skilled workers
items.reason: The writer proposes keeping fees for most courses.

items.prompt: In the second paragraph, the writer suggests that wider access to university may depend on
items.evidence: Clear information about repayment, I would argue, may do as much to widen access as abolishing fees altogether
items.reason: 'Explaining clearly how loans are repaid' paraphrases 'clear information about repayment'. Raising fees, entry grades and new universities are not mentioned.
options: A  raising fees for the most popular courses.
B  lowering the grades needed for entry.
C  explaining clearly how loans are repaid.
D  building more universities in poorer areas.

items.prompt: Why does the writer mention nursing and teaching?
items.evidence: require degrees but offer relatively modest salaries
items.reason: They illustrate essential careers that are not highly paid, weakening the 'graduates benefit personally' argument.
options: A  to show that average graduate earnings are a reliable guide
B  to give examples of essential careers that are not well paid
C  to argue that these courses should be shorter
D  to compare public and private universities

items.prompt: Which of the following best summarises the writer's position?
items.evidence: A more defensible position, in my opinion, lies between the two extremes
items.reason: The writer rejects both extremes (A and C) and proposes a reformed fee system rather than no change (B).
options: A  University education should be free for everyone.
B  The debate cannot be resolved, so the current system should stay as it is.
C  Taxpayers should cover the full cost of higher education.
D  Fees should be kept but designed to protect access and to direct public money well.

blocks.title: One developed body paragraph
blocks.mode: Independent classroom application after modelling; not a full Task 2 or Writing Screener
blocks.prompt: In many cities, the number of private cars is increasing. Some people think the government should charge drivers a fee to enter city centres. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write ONE body paragraph (about 140 words) that supports your view.
blocks.conditions: 12 minutes, independent. No model visible. Record word-bank use.
blocks.support: Frame: topic sentence (your view) → reason (lead to / result in) → specific example → concession (Admittedly, ... ; however, ...) → link back. Avoid 'good', 'bad', 'thing' and 'a lot of'.
blocks.extension: Add a hedged claim (arguably / it is likely that).
blocks.high_band: Concede one counter-point and rebut it with evidence or an example.
blocks.model_label: Illustrative classroom model for discussion only. Not a certified band answer.
blocks.model: In my view, charging drivers to enter city centres is one of the most effective ways to tackle congestion. When people must pay each time they drive into the centre, a significant proportion of them are likely to switch to buses, trains or bicycles, particularly for short journeys. This reduction in traffic would also have a beneficial effect on air quality, which is a major concern in many large cities. London provides a useful example: after a congestion charge was introduced, traffic in the charging zone fell noticeably in the first years of the scheme. Admittedly, such fees may place a heavier burden on low-income drivers; however, this drawback can be addressed by using the revenue to improve public transport. Arguably, therefore, the benefits of a charge outweigh its disadvantages.
checklist: Task Response: Is your position clear in the first sentence and supported throughout?
Lexical Resource: Have you replaced vague words, and are prepositions correct (lead to, stem from, effect on)?
Coherence and Cohesion: Does the paragraph develop one idea, with a concession that is then answered?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Are although/despite/however used with the correct structure?

blocks.title: Homework: precise and careful claims
blocks.mode: Homework; checked at the start of the next lesson
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-3: Complete each sentence with ONE word. Questions 4-6: Rewrite each sentence as instructed.

items.prompt: Rising house prices have resulted ______ more young adults living with their parents.
items.evidence: result in
items.reason: Fixed preposition.

items.prompt: Many cases of childhood obesity are ______ by a lack of physical activity.
items.evidence: be caused by
items.reason: Passive form.

items.prompt: ______ the high cost, many families choose private education.
items.evidence: despite + noun phrase
items.reason: 'In spite of' is also correct but uses three words; accept 'Despite' only for ONE word.

items.prompt: Make this claim more careful (hedge it): 'Online learning will replace schools.'
items.answer: It is unlikely that online learning will replace schools entirely, although it may become a larger part of education.
items.evidence: it is likely/unlikely that; may
items.reason: Accept any accurate hedged version (for example 'Online learning may to some extent replace ...'); it must not make an absolute prediction.

items.prompt: Replace the vague words: 'Tourism is bad for old cities because it causes a lot of problems.'
items.answer: Mass tourism can have a detrimental effect on historic city centres, for example by causing overcrowding and raising rents.
items.evidence: have a detrimental effect on + specific example
items.reason: Accept any version that replaces 'bad' and 'a lot of problems' with precise language and names at least one specific problem.

items.prompt: Write a concession and rebuttal about this view: 'Robots will take everyone's jobs.'
items.answer: Admittedly, automation will replace some routine jobs; however, it is unlikely to eliminate human work entirely, since it also creates new roles.
items.evidence: admittedly ... however
items.reason: Accept any accurate concession + rebuttal using 'admittedly ... however' or 'although'.

exit_ticket: Two cause-and-effect phrases with their prepositions:
A vague word I will stop using, and my precise replacement:
homework: Rewrite the conclusion of your last Task 2 essay, replacing every vague word with a precise one and hedging one claim.

blocks.title: Fresh check: which word fits exactly?
blocks.instructions: Choose the correct option, A, B, C or D, to complete each sentence. All the options are real English words.

items.prompt: Higher fuel prices have resulted ______ a rise in the number of people using buses.
items.evidence: result in
items.reason: 'Result' takes 'in' for consequences ('result from' gives the cause, which reverses the meaning here).

items.prompt: Local councils could ______ stricter rules on recycling.
items.evidence: introduce / implement rules
items.reason: You 'achieve' a goal, 'commit' a crime and 'perform' a task, but you introduce rules.

items.prompt: ______ the evidence, some politicians still deny that the policy has failed.
items.evidence: despite + noun phrase
items.reason: 'Although' and 'even though' need a clause; 'however' cannot introduce a noun phrase.

items.prompt: The writer wants to state their own view with caution: 'Genetic testing could, ______, do more harm than good.'
items.evidence: arguably = a careful claim the writer can defend
items.reason: 'Allegedly', 'supposedly' and 'reportedly' attribute the claim to other people.

blocks.title: Fresh check: homework
blocks.instructions: Do the statements agree with the claims of the writer? Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

stimulus.title: Does homework help?
paragraphs: It is often claimed that homework improves academic performance, and many parents judge a school partly by how much homework it sets. In my view, this belief is only partly justified. For older secondary students, there is reasonable evidence that well-designed homework is associated with better results, particularly when it consolidates what has been taught in class.

For younger children, however, the benefits are far less clear, and excessive homework may have a detrimental effect on sleep and family life. What matters, I would argue, is not the quantity of homework but its purpose. A short task that asks a child to read with a parent is arguably more valuable than an hour of repetitive exercises.

items.prompt: The common belief that homework raises achievement is entirely correct.
items.evidence: this belief is only partly justified
items.reason: 'Only partly justified' contradicts 'entirely correct'.

items.prompt: Homework can benefit older students when it reinforces classroom learning.
items.evidence: particularly when it consolidates what has been taught in class
items.reason: 'Reinforces classroom learning' paraphrases 'consolidates what has been taught in class'.

items.prompt: Teachers in most schools set too much homework.
items.evidence: The writer discusses excessive homework but not how much most schools set.
items.reason: No claim about most schools is made.

items.prompt: The amount of homework a child does is the most important factor.
items.evidence: What matters, I would argue, is not the quantity of homework but its purpose
items.reason: The writer says purpose matters, not quantity.
